clue.text: Club's language discussed in flyer

parts.note: a wood is the golf club with the big rounded head, once carved from persimmon

indicators.note: Something discussed is spoken aloud rather than written down, so the word beside it is wanted by ear.

parts.note: a pidgin is the makeshift language two peoples invent when they share no tongue, and it is said exactly like the bird

explanation.walkthrough: 'Club' wants to be a night out and is the golfer's kind. Two quite different spellings of one sound are what the second half turns on.
explanation.definitionFit: flyer → WOOD PIGEON: definition by example, the fat grey bird of British gardens standing in for the general idea of a thing that flies.

clue.text: Carry On Nurse's finale introduced by comedian

indicators.note: A finale is the closing item of a show, so it asks for the closing letter of the word beside it.

parts.note: a wag is a joker, the man always ready with a quip

indicators.note: An act introduced by a compere goes on after them, so this letter follows the man doing the introducing.

parts.note: the last letter of the word, and the clue's own apostrophe-s marks where it ends

explanation.walkthrough: Carry On Nurse is one of the British Carry On comedy films, which is why the title is italicised; splitting that title in two is the move the clue hides.
explanation.definitionFit: Carry On → WAGE: you wage a war or a campaign in the sense of carrying it on, the verb for keeping something in progress.

clue.text: Outstanding poem recited

indicators.note: To recite a piece is to say it out loud, so the sound of the word is what counts and not its spelling.

parts.note: a poem, especially a lofty one addressed to somebody or something, is an ode

explanation.walkthrough: Three letters against four, sharing only two of them: in a clue of three words the ear is the only thing you can use.
explanation.definitionFit: Outstanding → OWED: the sense of a bill still unsettled rather than the sense of excellent, which is the trap in a one-word definition.

clue.text: In favour of proposal initially addressing lewd, concerning advertising

parts.note: to be pro something is to be in favour of it
the proposal put before a meeting for debate is a motion

indicators.note: What happens initially happens at the very start, so only the opening letter of each word that follows is taken.

parts.note: the opening letters of the two words, taken in the order the clue gives them

explanation.walkthrough: The comma after 'lewd' does the hiding: it makes the surface a complaint about smut and disguises two ordinary words that are there only for their first letters.
explanation.definitionFit: concerning advertising → PROMOTIONAL: promotional material is material that promotes, the marketing sense of promotion rather than a rise in rank.

clue.text: Spin round, ultimately knackered: run's so long

parts.note: a spin at something is a go at it, one attempt
the round letter, drawn as a circle

indicators.note: What comes ultimately comes at the very end, so the final letter of the word beside it is all that is used.

parts.note: its final letter; knackered is British slang for worn out
in cricket a bye is a run scored when the batter never touches the ball

explanation.walkthrough: Four separate pieces inside seven letters, and the colon invites you to read 'knackered' as a description of a runner rather than as a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: so long → GOODBYE: 'so long' is the casual spoken farewell, an idiom meaning the parting word itself rather than any length of time.

clue.text: Ready and available beer, right?

parts.note: a drink that is available is on, as in on tap or on the menu
ale is the crossword's standard beer, three letters and endlessly useful
Rt is the abbreviation for right, as in the Rt Hon before a minister's name

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark sells 'beer, right?' as pub conversation, and that is exactly what stops those two words being read as two separate pieces of a build.
explanation.definitionFit: Ready → ON ALERT: the standing-by sense, watchful and waiting for something to happen, rather than ready meaning finished or prepared.

clue.text: A lot of land in limits of atlases' Iberia

indicators.note: The limits of a word are its outer edges, so you keep the opening and closing letter and drop everything between.

parts.note: the edges of the word, its first letter and its last
the same treatment of the peninsula Spain and Portugal share

explanation.walkthrough: One instruction has to reach across two words here, and the geography in the surface — atlases, Iberia — is there to keep you looking for a country instead of at letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A lot of land → ASIA: definition by example, the largest continent standing in for the general idea of a very great deal of land.

clue.text: Misadventures, as glue guns are wont to lead to?

definitions.meaning: the idiom: to come to one is to finish badly, the fate the villain meets in the last chapter

definitions.text: as glue guns are wont to lead to
definitions.meaning: read literally instead — what comes out of the nozzle leaves every join tacky

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is the setter admitting the second half is a joke rather than a dictionary sense, and both halves still land on the same two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Misadventures → STICKY ENDS by the idiom of coming to a bad end; the glue gun half is the phrase read literally, joins left tacky with adhesive.

clue.text: Apiarist's worried about dead evergreen

indicators.note: A dog worries a rag by shaking it, and letters shaken like that do not come back in the order they went in.
Sending one letter about the others drops it somewhere among them rather than leaving it at either end.

parts.note: an apiarist keeps bees, and the clue's apostrophe-s hands over a ninth letter for the mix
d is the standard abbreviation for dead, the one used on family trees

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a beekeeper fretting over a lost hive, so the last thing it invites you to do is count the letters of his job title. Nine of them, plus one, is the whole clue.
explanation.definitionFit: evergreen → ASPIDISTRA: the tough Victorian parlour plant keeps its leaves all year, so the noun names it by the class of plants it belongs to.

clue.text: Moan, flailing with grocer, wrestling thus?

indicators.note: Arms flailing go everywhere at once, so the letters beside the word land in no order you were handed.

parts.note: four letters lifted straight out of the clue, the comma after them the only hint they are fodder
six more, untouched, to be mixed in with the first four

explanation.walkthrough: A moaning grocer in a wrestling match is a good enough picture to stop you counting: ten letters in the clue, ten in the grid, and 'thus' pointing at a style rather than a sport.
explanation.definitionFit: wrestling thus → GRECO-ROMAN: the Olympic style that bans holds below the waist, so the phrase names a manner of fighting, not the sport itself.

clue.text: In retreat, Starmer largely ailing and weak

indicators.note: An army in retreat goes back the way it came, so these letters are read from the far end of the row instead.
Take the large part of a word and leave the remainder, which here means dropping its final letter.

parts.note: Keir Starmer is the British prime minister, and PM is the abbreviation for that office
ailing is ill, with the last of its three letters left off

explanation.walkthrough: Politics is the misdirection: a prime minister in retreat over a policy is a headline, not wordplay. Build the two short pieces first, then read them the other way.
explanation.definitionFit: weak → LIMP: the adjective for something drooping and without firmness, a limp handshake or limp lettuce, rather than the verb about walking.

clue.text: Incapable of satisfying demands — like the Bible, largely?

definitions.meaning: the diary sense: two people promised the same hour, so one of them is certain to be let down
the hyphenated phrase read literally — Old Testament and New, two collections bound as one volume

explanation.walkthrough: 'Largely' is the setter being honest: each Testament is itself a shelf of books, so the count of two only holds at the level everybody actually thinks of them.
explanation.definitionFit: One half is the diary sense, two commitments at one hour so neither can be met; the other reads the words literally, one volume made of two collections.

clue.text: Conspicuous chuckle: trouble getting on

parts.note: an overt act is done in the open where anyone can see it
the half-laugh as it is written down, three letters of quiet amusement
the ills of the world are its troubles, the noun rather than the adjective

explanation.walkthrough: The enumeration promises three words and the build supplies three pieces, but the seams fall in completely different places, which is the whole difficulty.
explanation.definitionFit: getting on → OVER THE HILL: both are gentle idioms for advancing age, past your best rather than simply older than you were.

clue.text: Sticking around, old policeman chatting online

indicators.note: To go around something is to sit on both sides of it, so the first word wraps itself about the letters that come next.

parts.note: sticking paper down is pasting it, and this is the word that does the wrapping
o is the standard abbreviation for old, as in the O of OAP
DC is a detective constable, a rank in a British police force

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sticking around' reads as one phrase meaning hanging about, which is why it is so hard to see that the first word is a wrapper and the second the instruction to wrap.
explanation.definitionFit: chatting online → PODCASTING: recording talk and publishing the episodes over the internet, so the loose phrase names the activity rather than defining it.

clue.text: Inflammation in it doesn't hurt

indicators.note: Something hurt has been knocked out of shape, and letters knocked out of shape do not stay in the order given.

parts.note: three tiny words, ten letters between them, and every one of the ten is used

explanation.walkthrough: 'Doesn't hurt' is such a natural phrase that it hides a whole anagram, and the fodder is the three words nobody stops to read as words.
explanation.definitionFit: Inflammation → TENDONITIS: definition by example, since it is the inflaming of a tendon in particular, one condition among many that end in -itis.

clue.text: Formerly a magazine

definitions.note: 'Formerly' is an adverb where the answer is an adjective — you would say a one-time champion, not a one-time it happened — and the setter is trading on the sense they share, at an earlier time.

parts.note: the indefinite article counts as one of a thing
Time is the American weekly news magazine, founded in 1923

explanation.walkthrough: Three words and nothing to grip: the trap is taking 'a magazine' for the definition and hunting through periodicals for a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Formerly → ONE-TIME: the crossword's usual way of marking a former holder of a title, the sense of something that was so at an earlier date.

clue.text: Adolescent's getting hot — and later, loud — somewhere in E England

indicators.note: Getting something is taking it in, so the letter named next goes inside the word in front of it.
The second insertion is made further along than the first, which is the only thing telling you where to drop it.

parts.note: a teen is an adolescent, and the clue's apostrophe-s supplies the final letter
H is the letter on the hot tap
f is forte in music, the instruction to play loudly

explanation.walkthrough: This is the flat drained marshland of Cambridgeshire and Lincolnshire, much of it below sea level — a region British solvers know by name and nobody else has to.
explanation.definitionFit: somewhere in E England → THE FENS: a definition by region, pointing at the low wetland district of the east rather than naming a town in it.

clue.text: Exotic dance with last and first characters showing musical flourish

indicators.note: Something exotic is foreign and unfamiliar, so the letters are to be made strange rather than left standing as they are.

parts.note: five letters lifted straight out of the clue
the characters are letters of the alphabet, whose last and first are Z and A

explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' wants to mean people in a story and 'last and first' wants to mean a running order; both belong to the alphabet instead.
explanation.definitionFit: musical flourish → CADENZA: the showy unaccompanied passage near the end of a concerto movement, where the soloist is left alone to display.

clue.text: One having, primarily, a terrifically healthy lifestyle; example: track eventer!

definitions.text: One having, primarily, a terrifically healthy lifestyle; example: track eventer!

indicators.note: What comes primarily comes first, so it is the opening letter of each word that follows which is wanted.

parts.note: the opening letters of those three words, in the order the clue sets them down
the same treatment carries on past the semicolon: three more words, three more openings

explanation.walkthrough: An &lit, so nothing is left over for a separate definition: read straight through, the sentence describes precisely the sort of person whose initials it has been spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight as the definition: someone with a healthy lifestyle who competes in track events is exactly what those initials spell out.

clue.text: Some beam at adorable fellow in jacket and tights

indicators.note: Some of a thing is a part of it, so what is wanted is a run of the letters in front of you and not whole words.

parts.note: seven consecutive letters, starting inside the first word and running on across both gaps

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is doing its own bit of hiding: the costume is the traje de luces, the sequinned suit of lights, and 'fellow' keeps you hunting for a man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: fellow in jacket and tights → MATADOR: the bullfighter's suit of lights is a short embroidered jacket over skin-tight breeches and stockings.

clue.text: Old President calling for some Imodium and Elastoplasts

indicators.note: Only some of what follows is used: one unbroken run of letters taken out of the middle, leaving the rest behind.

parts.note: the run starts at the end of the first brand name and stops early in the last; Elastoplast is the British name for a sticking plaster

explanation.walkthrough: A medicine cabinet makes a good hiding place: both brand names are long, and neither is the sort of word anyone scans for a spare statesman.
explanation.definitionFit: Old President → MANDELA: Nelson Mandela was President of South Africa from 1994 to 1999, so 'old' here means former rather than aged.

clue.text: Unaccompanied, like a swimming-pool clock

definitions.meaning: the everyday sense: doing the whole job on your own, with nobody else's help
the pace clock on a poolside wall carries one big sweep hand for swimmers to time their lengths by

explanation.walkthrough: The comma is the seam. The second half is a picture rather than a dictionary sense — a clock described by how many hands it happens to have.
explanation.definitionFit: Unaccompanied is the figurative sense, working alone; the poolside pace clock is the literal one, a face with one sweeping hand and no other.

clue.text: Going up to Reading, say, entertaining one that'll amuse you

indicators.note: In a down clue what goes up is read from the bottom of the column, so those letters arrive back to front.
To entertain a guest is to have them inside the house, so the piece named next sits within the other letters.

parts.note: two letters taken straight from the clue's own preposition
reading is one of the three Rs, the schoolroom trio with writing and arithmetic, so it is an example of an R
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.walkthrough: 'Going up to Reading' looks like a train journey to the Berkshire town, and the town has nothing to do with it. Turn the two small pieces round first, then let the third in.
explanation.definitionFit: that'll amuse you → RIOT: calling a person or a show a riot is the informal sense meaning hilarious, a long way from civil disorder.

clue.text: Verbally opposed requirement to play poker

indicators.note: Verbally means in speech, so what the clue hands over is a sound that has to be written down some other way.

parts.note: to be opposed to something is to be anti it, and that prefix said aloud lands on a different spelling

explanation.walkthrough: Two four-letter words a single vowel apart and belonging to different worlds: one is a stance and the other is money on the table.
explanation.definitionFit: requirement to play poker → ANTE: the compulsory chip every player puts in the pot before a card is dealt, so no stake means no hand.

clue.text: Everyman: old? Bless you! A little bit

parts.note: the setter signs these puzzles Everyman, and a setter referring to himself is I
o is the standard abbreviation for old
ta is the everyday British thank-you, what you say when somebody does you a small kindness

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a sneeze and a blessing. 'Everyman' is the setter's own name dropped into his clue, and he is entitled to use it as a letter standing for himself.
explanation.definitionFit: A little bit → IOTA: the smallest letter of the Greek alphabet, borrowed to mean the tiniest imaginable quantity of anything at all.

clue.text: Challenged Soviet line that's set

indicators.note: To challenge something is to call it into question, and letters called into question will not stand in the order they were given.

parts.note: six letters straight from the clue, with the Cold War surface doing the hiding
four more, and ten in total is exactly what the grid is asking for

explanation.walkthrough: 'Challenged Soviet line' reads as a news headline, which is the trick: those words are fodder rather than politics, and the definition is the small word left looking like part of the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: set → TELEVISION: the appliance sense, the set in the corner of the room, where the noun names the whole box rather than anything being set.

clue.text: I ask you to leave quietly

parts.note: to leave a place is to go
sh is the noise you make when asking for quiet

explanation.walkthrough: 'I ask you' looks like the setter addressing the solver directly, and is really a mild explosion of disbelief, the sort said with the hands in the air.
explanation.definitionFit: I ask you → GOSH: both are exclamations of surprise or exasperation, so a whole phrase stands in for a single word of the same feeling.

clue.text: At year's end, an unstimulating brew — mostly that?

indicators.note: Most of a word is all of it bar the end, so the final letter is dropped before the piece is used.

parts.note: December is the month the year finishes in, and Dec is its abbreviation
the indefinite article, which in wordplay is simply the letter
a flat drink has lost its fizz and its lift
the brew is tea, with the last of its three letters left off

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue before the dash is wordplay and a description at once: 'that?' points back at 'an unstimulating brew' and asks what it is. 'A flat' is a musical key too, and that is the joke the surface leans on.
explanation.definitionFit: that? → DECAF LATTE: 'that' points back at the unstimulating brew just described, a milky coffee with the caffeine taken out.
